{{DISPLAYTITLE:Building things from constructors}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Inductive types and recursors}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Most of the things Lean reasons about (numbers, lists, trees, true and false) are made in
one way: by naming a few rules for making values and declaring that nothing else counts.
This page explains that idea, how Lean takes such values apart again, and the principle of
recursion that Lean derives from the rules.

== A type given by its rules ==

The natural numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, ... can be described by two rules. Zero is a natural
number. If n is a natural number, so is the next one after n, its '''successor'''. Every
natural number is reached from zero by applying the second rule some finite number of
times, and nothing else is a natural number.

Lean's own definition says exactly this. Asked to print it,

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#print Nat
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 answers:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
inductive Nat : Type
number of parameters: 0
constructors:
Nat.zero : Nat
Nat.succ : Nat → Nat
</pre>

A type defined this way is an '''inductive type'''. Its rules are its '''constructors''':
here <code>Nat.zero</code>, which needs nothing, and <code>Nat.succ</code>, which takes one
natural number and makes the next. Three is <code>Nat.succ (Nat.succ (Nat.succ
Nat.zero))</code>, and the numeral 3 names the same number. The values of an
inductive type are exactly the ones its constructors make; it has no others.<ref name="tpil-ind">Jeremy
Avigad, Leonardo de Moura, Soonho Kong and Sebastian Ullrich, ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4''
(online edition for Lean 4.33.0, lean-lang.org), chapter 7, "Inductive Types".
https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Inductive-Types/</ref>

This is not one device among many. Functions, universes and quotient types are built into
Lean; every other type is an inductive type or is defined from functions, universes and
inductive types.<ref name="ref-ind">''The
Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0 (lean-lang.org, 2026), section 4.4,
"Inductive Types". https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Inductive-Types/</ref>

== Lists and trees ==

The same pattern makes a list. A list is either empty, or a first item followed by a list.
Asked for <code>#print List</code>, Lean shows its own definition of lists in the same form:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
inductive List.{u} : Type u → Type u
number of parameters: 1
constructors:
List.nil : {α : Type u} → List α
List.cons : {α : Type u} → α → List α → List α
</pre>

The letter α stands for the type of the items, so the one definition gives lists of numbers,
lists of words and lists of lists. The list <code>[1, 2]</code> is <code>cons</code> of 1
onto <code>cons</code> of 2 onto the empty list <code>nil</code>.

A tree with numbers at its branch points takes two rules of the same kind, and the size of a
tree is a short definition on top of them:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
inductive Tree where
  | leaf : Tree
  | node : Tree → Nat → Tree → Tree

def Tree.size : Tree → Nat
  | leaf       => 0
  | node l _ r => l.size + 1 + r.size

#eval (Tree.node (Tree.node Tree.leaf 5 Tree.leaf) 7 Tree.leaf).size
</pre>

A leaf carries nothing. A node carries a left tree, a number and a right tree. Because a
constructor may take values of the very type being defined, a few lines describe trees of
every finite size. The <code>#eval</code> line asks for the size of a tree with two nodes,
and Lean prints <code>2</code>.

== Taking values apart ==

To use a value of an inductive type, a definition asks which constructor made it and what
was put into it. This is '''pattern matching'''. The definition of <code>Tree.size</code>
above has one line per constructor: a leaf has size zero, and a node has the sizes of its
two subtrees plus one for itself.

Lean checks that every constructor is covered. A definition that forgets one is refused:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def isZero : Nat → Bool
  | 0 => true
</pre>

Lean answers <code>Missing cases:</code> and shows the shape left unhandled,
<code>(Nat.succ _)</code>: a number made by the successor rule, with anything at all inside.
The check is possible because a natural number can only have come from one of the two rules.
A definition that handles both handles every number.

== The recursion principle ==

From the constructors alone, Lean derives one more thing: a '''recursion principle''', also
called the type's '''recursor'''. For the natural numbers, <code>#check Nat.rec</code> prints:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
Nat.rec.{u} {motive : Nat → Sort u} (zero : motive Nat.zero) (succ : (n : Nat) → motive n → motive n.succ) (t : Nat) :
  motive t
</pre>

In plain words: to produce something for every natural number <code>t</code>, supply what it
is for zero, and a way to obtain it for the successor of <code>n</code> from <code>n</code>
and from what it is for <code>n</code>. The word ''motive'' names the thing being produced,
which may be different for each number. The recursor then delivers it for every number,
because every number is zero followed by finitely many successors.

The recursion principle does two jobs, and the Lean Language Reference describes it in both
roles.<ref name="ref-ind" /> As computation, it defines functions: Lean translates the
structurally recursive functions of [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Functions that always
finish|functions that always finish]] into uses of it, and that is how the Lean kernel knows
they end. As logic, where the thing produced for each number is a proof, it is proof by
induction: prove a statement for zero, show that it passes from each number to the next, and
it holds for all of them.<ref name="tpil-ind" />
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Induction, as the machine sees it|Induction, as the machine
sees it]] follows that second job.

Every inductive type has a recursor, with one case per constructor. The type
<code>Bool</code> of true and false has two constructors that take nothing, and
<code>#check Bool.rec</code> shows that its recursor asks for one answer for
<code>false</code> and one for <code>true</code>. That is a choice between two cases and
nothing more.

== Structures: the one-constructor case ==

Often a value is several things kept together: a point is an x and a y. A '''structure''' is
an inductive type with exactly one constructor, whose arguments are called its
'''fields'''.<ref name="ref-ind" />

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
structure Point where
  x : Nat
  y : Nat

#eval (Point.mk 3 4).y
#print Point
</pre>

The <code>#eval</code> line prints <code>4</code>. The <code>#print</code> line lists the
fields <code>Point.x</code> and <code>Point.y</code> and the single constructor
<code>Point.mk (x y : Nat) : Point</code>. For structures, Lean adds conveniences: a function
that reads each field, a way to write values by field name, and a way to extend one
structure with another. These add no power. Everything a structure does could be done with a
one-constructor inductive type, and the reference manual says so.<ref name="ref-ind" />

== What the idea gives ==

Defining a type by its constructors fixes three things at once. How to make its values is
the list of constructors. How to take them apart is pattern matching, which Lean checks for
completeness. How to reason about all of them is the recursion principle, which Lean derives
without being told, and which serves both to define functions and as the principle of
induction.
